title: "Module 7 — Shape and univariate review"
subtitle: "Data Description | Part II — Summarising one variable"
date-modified: 2026-10-17

**The business question.** "The Wandering Fork" has a mean daily
revenue of €628.34 and a standard deviation of €137.09 (Harbour,
30 days) — but knowing *how much* the data spreads out says nothing
about *how* it spreads out: is it balanced evenly around its center,
or lopsided with a longer tail in one direction? **Skewness**
indicators answer exactly that question, and they close the loop on
what the mean, median, and mode (Module 4) were quietly hinting at
all along. This module also consolidates the entire univariate
toolkit (Modules 3–6) into one complete workflow.
We start with three trucks that Module 6 cannot tell apart — same
mean, same standard deviation — small enough to compute by hand, and
only then write the formulas.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you will be able to:

- Explain what a symmetric, right-skewed, and left-skewed
  distribution look like, and how the mean, median, and mode
  typically order themselves in each case.
- Compute the Fisher-Pearson sample skewness coefficient for a small
  dataset with a cubed-deviation table, explain why the deviations are
  cubed, and read its formula aloud as a sentence.
- Compute the Pearson skewness coefficient (mode and median forms) and
  the Yule-Kendall skewness coefficient by hand, and recognize that
  different formulas can disagree in sign or magnitude for
  near-symmetric data.
- Read skewness directly off a histogram or boxplot.
- Describe kurtosis in words (leptokurtic, mesokurtic, platykurtic)
  and tell it apart from skewness.
- Write a skewness formula in symbols from a description in words.

## Theory

### Same mean, same spread, different shapes

Three Wandering Fork trucks recorded their revenue on a few ordinary
days at three different pitches. The numbers are a simplified extract
chosen so that you can compute everything by hand.

| Truck (pitch) | Daily revenue (€) | Days | Mean (€) | Std. dev. $s$ (€) |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Station | 510, 570, 600, 600, 630, 690 | 6 | 600 | 60 |
| Stadium | 550, 550, 580, 630, 690 | 5 | 600 | 60 |
| Market | 510, 570, 620, 650, 650 | 5 | 600 | 60 |

With the tools of Modules 4 and 6 — the mean and the standard
deviation — the three trucks look **identical**: €600 on an average
day, give or take about €60. Are they really the same business? For
which truck would "a typical day is €600" be most misleading, and in
which direction? Look at the figure before computing anything (start
with step 1).

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
station = [510, 570, 600, 600, 630, 690]
stadium = [550, 550, 580, 630, 690]
market = [510, 570, 620, 650, 650]

function shape(xs) {
  const n = xs.length;
  const sorted = [...xs].sort((a, b) => a - b);
  const mean = xs.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) / n;
  const median = n % 2 ? sorted[(n - 1) / 2]
    : (sorted[n / 2 - 1] + sorted[n / 2]) / 2;
  const counts = new Map();
  xs.forEach(x => counts.set(x, (counts.get(x) || 0) + 1));
  const top = Math.max(...counts.values());
  const modes = [...counts].filter(([, c]) => c === top).map(([v]) => v);
  const mode = top > 1 && modes.length === 1 ? modes[0] : null;
  const dev = sorted.map(x => x - mean);
  const s = Math.sqrt(dev.reduce((a, d) => a + d * d, 0) / (n - 1));
  const cube10 = dev.map(d => (d / 10) ** 3);
  const sumCube10 = cube10.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
  const skew = n / ((n - 1) * (n - 2)) * sumCube10 / (s / 10) ** 3;
  const quart = p => {
    const pos = (n + 1) * p, k = Math.floor(pos);
    const lo = sorted[k - 1], hi = sorted[Math.min(k, n - 1)];
    return lo + (pos - k) * (hi - lo);
  };
  const q1 = quart(0.25), q3 = quart(0.75);
  const yk = (q3 + q1 - 2 * median) / (q3 - q1);
  return {n, sorted, mean, median, mode, dev, s, cube10, sumCube10, skew,
    q1, q3, yk, min: sorted[0], max: sorted[n - 1]};
}

num = (v, d = 0) => (v < 0 ? "−" : "") + Math.abs(v).toFixed(d)
signed = (v, d = 0) => (v > 0 ? "+" : "") + num(v, d)

shapeTrucks = [["Station", station], ["Stadium", stadium],
  ["Market", market]].map(([name, xs]) => ({name, st: shape(xs)}))

viewof shapeStep = {
  const labels = ["1 · Dots", "2 · Mean, median, mode", "3 · Cubes",
    "4 · Quartiles"];
  const form = html`<form class="ojs-step-picker">Show: ${labels.map((l, i) =>
    html`<label> <input type="radio" name="shapeStep" value="${i + 1}"
      ${i === 0 ? "checked" : ""}> ${l} </label>`)}</form>`;
  form.value = 1;
  form.oninput = () => {
    form.value = +form.querySelector("input:checked").value;
  };
  return form;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const W = 660, BLUE = "steelblue", ORANGE = "darkorange";
  const GREEN = "seagreen", PURPLE = "mediumpurple";
  const POS = "#5cb85c", NEG = "#d9534f";
  const panel = 110;
  let g = "";

  if (shapeStep !== 3) {
    const x = v => 120 + (v - 480) * (W - 150) / (720 - 480);
    const H = 3 * panel + 50;
    shapeTrucks.forEach(({name, st}, k) => {
      const top = 10 + k * panel, y0 = top + 60;
      g += `<text x="10" y="${y0}" fill="currentColor"
        font-weight="bold">${name}</text>`;
      if (shapeStep === 2) {
        const marks = [["mode", st.mode, PURPLE, "2 3", 12],
                       ["median", st.median, GREEN, "", 26],
                       ["mean", st.mean, ORANGE, "6 4", 40]];
        marks.forEach(([label, v, c, dash, dy]) => {
          g += `<line x1="${x(v)}" x2="${x(v)}" y1="${top + dy - 10}"
            y2="${y0 + 10}" stroke="${c}" stroke-width="2"
            stroke-dasharray="${dash}"/>`;
          g += `<text x="${x(v) + 5}" y="${top + dy}" fill="${c}"
            font-size="12">${label} ${num(v)}</text>`;
        });
      }
      const seen = new Map();
      st.sorted.forEach(v => {
        const r = seen.get(v) || 0;
        seen.set(v, r + 1);
        g += `<circle cx="${x(v)}" cy="${y0 - 14 * r}" r="6"
          fill="${BLUE}"/>`;
      });
      if (shapeStep === 4) {
        const yb = y0 + 22;
        g += `<line x1="${x(st.min)}" x2="${x(st.q1)}" y1="${yb}"
          y2="${yb}" stroke="currentColor"/>`;
        g += `<line x1="${x(st.q3)}" x2="${x(st.max)}" y1="${yb}"
          y2="${yb}" stroke="currentColor"/>`;
        g += `<rect x="${x(st.q1)}" y="${yb - 8}"
          width="${x(st.q3) - x(st.q1)}" height="16" fill="${BLUE}"
          fill-opacity="0.25" stroke="${BLUE}"/>`;
        g += `<line x1="${x(st.median)}" x2="${x(st.median)}"
          y1="${yb - 8}" y2="${yb + 8}" stroke="${GREEN}"
          stroke-width="3"/>`;
        g += `<text x="10" y="${y0 + 44}" fill="currentColor"
          font-size="12">Me − Q1 = ${num(st.median - st.q1)},
          Q3 − Me = ${num(st.q3 - st.median)}</text>`;
      }
    });
    for (let t = 500; t <= 700; t += 50) {
      g += `<line x1="${x(t)}" x2="${x(t)}" y1="${H - 30}" y2="${H - 24}"
        stroke="currentColor"/>`;
      g += `<text x="${x(t)}" y="${H - 10}" text-anchor="middle"
        fill="currentColor" font-size="12">€${t}</text>`;
    }
    g += `<line x1="${x(480)}" x2="${x(720)}" y1="${H - 30}" y2="${H - 30}"
      stroke="currentColor"/>`;
    return html`<svg viewBox="0 0 ${W} ${H}" width="100%" role="img"
      aria-label="Daily revenue of the Station, Stadium and Market trucks">
      ${g}</svg>`;
  }

  const k = 220 / 729, cx = 340, H = 3 * panel;
  shapeTrucks.forEach(({name, st}, t) => {
    const top = 10 + t * panel;
    g += `<text x="10" y="${top + 30}" fill="currentColor"
      font-weight="bold">${name}</text>`;
    g += `<line x1="${cx}" x2="${cx}" y1="${top}" y2="${top + 82}"
      stroke="${ORANGE}" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/>`;
    st.cube10.forEach((c, i) => {
      const y = top + 6 + i * 13, len = Math.abs(c) * k;
      const col = c > 0 ? POS : c < 0 ? NEG : "currentColor";
      if (c !== 0) {
        g += `<rect x="${c > 0 ? cx : cx - len}" y="${y - 5}"
          width="${len}" height="10" fill="${col}"/>`;
      }
      g += `<text x="${c >= 0 ? cx + len + 6 : cx - len - 6}" y="${y + 4}"
        text-anchor="${c >= 0 ? "start" : "end"}" fill="${col}"
        font-size="11">${signed(c)}</text>`;
    });
    g += `<text x="10" y="${top + 50}" fill="currentColor"
      font-size="12">sum = ${signed(st.sumCube10)}</text>`;
  });
  return html`<svg viewBox="0 0 ${W} ${H}" width="100%" role="img"
    aria-label="Cubed deviations, in tens of euros, of the three trucks">
    ${g}</svg>`;
}

//| echo: false
{
  const order = st => {
    const m = [["mode", st.mode], ["median", st.median], ["mean", st.mean]];
    if (m.every(([, v]) => v === st.mean)) return "all three are equal";
    return m.sort((a, b) => a[1] - b[1]).map(([l]) => l).join(" < ");
  };
  const line = ({name, st}) => shapeStep === 1
    ? `${name}: ${st.n} days from €${st.min} to €${st.max}, mean €${num(st.mean)}, s = €${num(st.s)}.`
    : shapeStep === 2
    ? `${name}: mode ${num(st.mode)}, median ${num(st.median)}, mean ${num(st.mean)} — ${order(st)}.`
    : shapeStep === 3
    ? `${name}: cubed deviations (tens of €) ${st.cube10.map(c => signed(c)).join(", ")}, sum ${signed(st.sumCube10)}; SKEW = ${st.n}/${(st.n - 1) * (st.n - 2)} × ${num(st.sumCube10)}/${num((st.s / 10) ** 3)} = ${num(st.skew, 2)}.`
    : `${name}: Q1 = ${num(st.q1)}, Me = ${num(st.median)}, Q3 = ${num(st.q3)}; YK = ${num(st.q3 + st.q1 - 2 * st.median)}/${num(st.q3 - st.q1)} = ${num(st.yk, 2)}.`;
  return html`<p><em>${shapeTrucks.map(t => html`${line(t)}<br>`)}</em></p>`;
}
```

### Symmetry and skewness

**Try it.** For each truck, sort the values, then find the mean, the
median and the mode (Module 4). Put the three in increasing order.

| Truck | Sorted values (€) | Mean | Median $Me$ | Mode $Mo$ | Order |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Station | 510, 570, 600, 600, 630, 690 | ? | ? | ? | ? |
| Stadium | 550, 550, 580, 630, 690 | ? | ? | ? | ? |
| Market | 510, 570, 620, 650, 650 | ? | ? | ? | ? |

Then: on which side of the bulk of the days is each truck's one
"unusual" day?

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Try it — check your answer
| Truck | Mean | Median $Me$ | Mode $Mo$ | Order |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Station | 600 | $(600+600)/2 = 600$ | 600 | all equal |
| Stadium | 600 | 580 | 550 | $Mo < Me < \bar{x}$ |
| Market | 600 | 620 | 650 | $\bar{x} < Me < Mo$ |

Station is balanced: 510 and 690 are each €90 from 600. Stadium's
unusual day is a **high** one (690, a match day): it pulls the mean up,
above the median, which is above the most frequent value. Market's
unusual day is a **low** one (510, a rainy day): everything flips. The
mean always moves toward the long tail, because it uses every value;
the median and the mode do not.
:::

**See it.** Step 2 of the figure draws the three centres as vertical
lines. For Station they sit on top of each other; for Stadium the mean
(orange) is pulled to the right of the median (green) and the mode
(purple); Market is the mirror image.

In plain words: symmetric = balanced; right-skewed = tail drags to
the right (a few exceptionally high values); left-skewed = tail
drags to the left (a few exceptionally low values). The mean is
dragged toward the tail, the median less, the mode not at all.

::: {.callout-note}
#### Definition — symmetry and skewness
A distribution is **symmetric** if its left and right halves,
measured from the center, are mirror images of each other; in that
case the mean, median, and mode coincide. A distribution is
**skewed** when one tail is longer or fatter than the other.
**Right-skewed** (positive skew) means a longer tail toward high
values, typically pulling the mean above the median above the mode
($\bar{x} > Me > Mo$). **Left-skewed** (negative skew) is the mirror
case, with a longer tail toward low values ($\bar{x} < Me < Mo$).
:::

### Fisher-Pearson sample skewness coefficient

The order of the three centres gives a direction, not a size. To use
**every** day, start again from the deviations of Module 6.

**Try it.** Stadium truck ($n = 5$, $\bar{x} = 600$, $s = 60$). We will
divide each deviation by $s$, so the euros cancel; that means you may
count the deviations in **tens of euros**, where $s = 6$.

| Day | $x_i$ (€) | $x_i-\bar{x}$ (€) | In tens of € | Cubed | Sign |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|:---:|
| 1 | 550 | ? | ? | ? | ? |
| 2 | 550 | ? | ? | ? | ? |
| 3 | 580 | ? | ? | ? | ? |
| 4 | 630 | ? | ? | ? | ? |
| 5 | 690 | ? | ? | ? | ? |
| **Total** | **3,000** | **?** | | **?** | |

1. Fill the deviation column and check that it adds up to 0
   (Module 6).
2. Divide each deviation by 10, cube it (e.g. $(-5)^3 = -125$), and add
   up the cubes.
3. Which single day decides the sign of the total?
4. Computed for you (calculator step): divide the total by
   $s^3 = 6^3 = 216$, then multiply by $\frac{5}{4 \times 3} =
   \frac{5}{12}$.

Your turn: build the same table for Market (510, 570, 620, 650, 650)
and for Station.

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Try it — check your answer
**Stadium**

| Day | $x_i$ | $x_i-\bar{x}$ | In tens of € | Cubed | Sign |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|:---:|
| 1 | 550 | −50 | −5 | −125 | − |
| 2 | 550 | −50 | −5 | −125 | − |
| 3 | 580 | −20 | −2 | −8 | − |
| 4 | 630 | 30 | 3 | 27 | + |
| 5 | 690 | 90 | 9 | 729 | + |
| **Total** | **3,000** | **0** | | **498** | **+** |

Day 5 alone (+729) outweighs the three negative days together
($-125-125-8 = -258$). Then $498/216 \approx 2.306$ and
$\frac{5}{12} \times 2.306 \approx 0.96$: Stadium's Fisher-Pearson
skewness is about **+0.96**, a clear right skew.

**Market:** deviations −90, −30, 20, 50, 50; in tens −9, −3, 2, 5, 5;
cubes −729, −27, 8, 125, 125; total **−498**, so the skewness is about
**−0.96** — the same size, opposite sign.

**Station:** deviations in tens −9, −3, 0, 0, 3, 9; cubes −729, −27, 0,
0, 27, 729; total **0**, so the skewness is **0**: perfectly symmetric.
:::

**Why cube and not square?** In Module 6 we squared the deviations to
remove their signs — perfect for measuring distance, useless for
direction: Stadium and Market have exactly the same squares, hence the
same $s$. Cubing keeps the sign (a negative number cubed stays
negative) and makes the far days dominate ($9^3 = 729$ but
$2^3 = 8$), so the total tells you **which side the long tail is on**.

**See it.** Step 3 of the figure draws each cube as a bar from the
mean: red to the left, green to the right. Stadium's single long green
bar wins; Market's single long red bar wins; Station's bars cancel in
pairs.

In plain words: measure each deviation in standard deviations, cube
those standardized deviations (so direction matters), and average them
with a small-sample correction. The correction factor
$\frac{n}{(n-1)(n-2)}$ matters most for small samples and becomes
negligible for large ones.

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Formula — Fisher-Pearson sample skewness coefficient
The primary skewness measure used in this course is the
**adjusted Fisher-Pearson standardized moment coefficient**, which is
what Excel's `SKEW` function computes:
$$
SKEW = \frac{n}{(n-1)(n-2)} \sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left(\frac{x_i-\bar{x}}{s}\right)^3.
$$
This standardizes every deviation from the mean (dividing by $s$, so
the result is unit-free), cubes it (so, unlike variance, positive and
negative deviations do *not* cancel and large deviations dominate),
and averages the result with a small-sample correction factor. A
value near $0$ signals near-symmetry; positive means right-skewed;
negative means left-skewed.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
#### Notation decoder — Fisher-Pearson sample skewness coefficient
| Symbol | Read aloud | In our example (Stadium) |
|---|---|---|
| $SKEW$ | "skew" | about +0.96 |
| $n$ | "n" | 5 days |
| $\frac{n}{(n-1)(n-2)}$ | "n over n minus 1 times n minus 2" | $\frac{5}{4\times3} = \frac{5}{12} \approx 0.417$ |
| $x_i$ | "x sub i" | the value on day $i$, e.g. $x_5 = 690$ |
| $\bar{x}$ | "x-bar" | the mean, 600 |
| $s$ | "s" | the standard deviation, 60 (6 in tens of €) |
| $\frac{x_i-\bar{x}}{s}$ | "x sub i minus x-bar, over s" | the deviation in standard deviations: −0.83, −0.83, −0.33, 0.5, 1.5 |
| $\left(\cdots\right)^3$ | "cubed" | e.g. $1.5^3 = 3.375$ (that is, $729/216$) |
| $\sum_{i=1}^{n}$ | "add up, for i from 1 to n" | $498/216 \approx 2.306$ |

**Whole formula as a sentence:** "the skewness is the sum, over all
$n$ days, of each day's deviation from the mean measured in standard
deviations and cubed, multiplied by the small-sample factor $n$ over
$(n-1)(n-2)$."
:::

### Alternative asymmetry coefficients

The Fisher-Pearson coefficient needs every raw value. Two shortcuts
need only a few summary numbers you already know.

**Try it — Pearson.** For Stadium and Market ($\bar{x} = 600$,
$s = 60$, medians and modes from the first Try it):

| Truck | Mean − mode (€) | Divided by $s$ | Mean − median (€) | 3 × that, divided by $s$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Stadium | ? | ? | ? | ? |
| Market | ? | ? | ? | ? |

**Try it — Yule-Kendall.** **Recall.** You computed quartiles in
[Module 5](module-05.qmd) with the position $(n+1)p$ and
interpolation: for $n = 5$, $Q_1$ sits at position $6 \times 0.25 =
1.5$ (halfway between the 1st and 2nd sorted values) and $Q_3$ at
position $6 \times 0.75 = 4.5$ (halfway between the 4th and 5th).

| Truck | $Q_1$ | $Me$ | $Q_3$ | $Me-Q_1$ | $Q_3-Me$ | (2nd gap − 1st gap) ÷ $(Q_3-Q_1)$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Stadium | ? | 580 | ? | ? | ? | ? |
| Market | ? | 620 | ? | ? | ? | ? |

Is each median closer to $Q_1$ or to $Q_3$?

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Try it — check your answer
**Pearson.**

| Truck | Mean − mode | Divided by $s$ | Mean − median | 3 × that, divided by $s$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Stadium | $600-550 = 50$ | $50/60 \approx 0.83$ | 20 | $60/60 = 1.00$ |
| Market | $600-650 = -50$ | $\approx -0.83$ | −20 | $-1.00$ |

**Yule-Kendall.** Stadium: $Q_1 = (550+550)/2 = 550$,
$Q_3 = (630+690)/2 = 660$. Market: $Q_1 = (510+570)/2 = 540$,
$Q_3 = (650+650)/2 = 650$.

| Truck | $Q_1$ | $Me$ | $Q_3$ | $Me-Q_1$ | $Q_3-Me$ | (2nd gap − 1st gap) ÷ $(Q_3-Q_1)$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Stadium | 550 | 580 | 660 | 30 | 80 | $50/110 \approx 0.45$ |
| Market | 540 | 620 | 650 | 80 | 30 | $-50/110 \approx -0.45$ |

Stadium's median is closer to $Q_1$: the upper quarter of the data is
more spread out, a sign of right skew. All three shortcuts agree in
sign with the Fisher-Pearson value (+0.96 / −0.96), but not in size:
0.83, 1.00 and 0.45 for the same truck.
:::

**See it.** Step 4 of the figure draws each truck's box from $Q_1$ to
$Q_3$ with the median as a green bar: Stadium's median hugs the left
edge of its box, Market's hugs the right edge, Station's sits in the
middle.

In plain words: the Pearson coefficient counts how many standard
deviations the mean has been pulled away from the mode (or, three
times, from the median); the Yule-Kendall coefficient checks whether
the median sits closer to $Q_1$ or to $Q_3$ inside the box.

::: {.callout-note}
#### Definition — alternative asymmetry coefficients
Two simpler, complementary measures are also common. The **Pearson
skewness coefficient** compares the mean to the mode, rescaled by the
standard deviation. The **Yule-Kendall skewness coefficient** instead
compares how the median sits between $Q_1$ and $Q_3$, using only the
five-number summary from Module 5 — useful when the mode is hard to
pin down or the data is only available as a boxplot.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Formula — Pearson and Yule-Kendall coefficients
$$
\text{Pearson asymmetry} = \frac{\bar{x}-Mo}{s},
\qquad\qquad
YK = \frac{Q_3+Q_1-2\,Me}{Q_3-Q_1}.
$$
When the mode is not well defined (raw continuous data, no repeated
value), use **Pearson's median form**, $3(\bar{x}-Me)/s$, which swaps
the mode for the median. The Pearson coefficient asks "how many
standard deviations separate the mean from the mode (or median)?"
The Yule-Kendall coefficient asks "is the median closer to $Q_1$ or
to $Q_3$?" — if $Me$ sits closer to $Q_1$
than to $Q_3$, the upper quarter of the data is more spread out,
which is itself a sign of right skew, and vice versa.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
#### Notation decoder — Pearson and Yule-Kendall coefficients
| Symbol | Read aloud | In our example (Stadium) |
|---|---|---|
| $\bar{x}$ | "x-bar" | the mean, 600 |
| $Mo$ | "the mode" | 550 (the value seen twice) |
| $s$ | "s" | 60 |
| $\frac{\bar{x}-Mo}{s}$ | "x-bar minus the mode, over s" | $50/60 \approx 0.83$ |
| $Me$ | "the median" | 580 |
| $3(\bar{x}-Me)/s$ | "three times x-bar minus the median, over s" | $3 \times 20/60 = 1.00$ |
| $Q_1$, $Q_3$ | "Q one", "Q three" | 550 and 660 |
| $Q_3+Q_1-2\,Me$ | "Q three plus Q one minus twice the median" | $660+550-1{,}160 = 50$, the same as $(Q_3-Me)-(Me-Q_1) = 80-30$ |
| $Q_3-Q_1$ | "Q three minus Q one" (the IQR) | 110 |
| $YK$ | "Yule-Kendall" | $50/110 \approx 0.45$ |

**Whole formula as a sentence:** "the Pearson coefficient is the gap
between the mean and the mode, measured in standard deviations; the
Yule-Kendall coefficient is how much longer the upper half of the box
is than the lower half, as a share of the whole box."
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
Different skewness formulas can genuinely disagree in sign or
magnitude, especially for near-symmetric data where all the values
involved are close to each other and small estimation differences
get amplified by division. Always state **which formula** you used
when reporting a skewness value — "the Fisher-Pearson skewness is
+0.034" is a precise, checkable claim; "the skewness is positive" is
not, unless the formula is named.
:::

### Reading skew from a chart

**Try it.** Here are the three five-number summaries (Station's
quartiles are at positions 1.75 and 5.25, since $n = 6$). Sketch the
three boxplots on one axis, or look at step 4 of the figure.

| Truck | Min | $Q_1$ | $Me$ | $Q_3$ | Max | Longer whisker | Median closer to | Skew |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---|---|
| Station | 510 | 555 | 600 | 645 | 690 | ? | ? | ? |
| Stadium | 550 | 550 | 580 | 660 | 690 | ? | ? | ? |
| Market | 510 | 540 | 620 | 650 | 650 | ? | ? | ? |

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Try it — check your answer
| Truck | Longer whisker | Median closer to | Skew |
|---|---|---|---|
| Station | neither (45 and 45) | the middle (45 and 45) | symmetric |
| Stadium | right (0 vs 30) | $Q_1$ (30 vs 80) | right |
| Market | left (30 vs 0) | $Q_3$ (80 vs 30) | left |

Both clues point the same way: the long side of the boxplot is the
side of the long tail.
:::

**See it.** In step 4, Stadium's box and whiskers stretch to the right
of its median; Market's stretch to the left. On a histogram, the same
truck would show a pile of bars on one side and a thin tail on the
other (see [Visual intuition](#visual-intuition)).

In plain words: the skew is on the side where the picture is
stretched out — the longer tail of the histogram, the longer whisker
and the wider half of the box of the boxplot.

### Kurtosis (conceptual only)

**Try it.** A fourth truck, at the Park pitch, also has mean €600 and
$s = €60$, and it is symmetric too (its skewness is 0). Compare it with
Station.

| Truck | Values (€) | Days within €30 of the mean | Farthest day from the mean (€) |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Station | 510, 570, 600, 600, 630, 690 | ? | ? |
| Park | 530, 550, 560, 640, 650, 670 | ? | ? |

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Try it — check your answer
| Truck | Days within €30 of the mean | Farthest day from the mean (€) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Station | 4 (570, 600, 600, 630) | 90 |
| Park | 0 | 70 |

Same mean, same $s$, same skewness — yet Station has a sharp peak at
600 *and* longer tails (510, 690), while Park is flat, with no day near
the centre and no far-out day. That remaining difference is what
kurtosis describes: Station leans **leptokurtic**, Park
**platykurtic**.
:::

**See it.** The two trucks on one number line (each • is one day):

| Truck | 510 | 530 | 550 | 560 | 570 | 600 | 630 | 640 | 650 | 670 | 690 |
|---|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| Station | • | | | | • | •• | • | | | | • |
| Park | | • | • | • | | | | • | • | • | |

In plain words: skewness asks "is one tail longer?"; kurtosis asks
"is there a sharp peak with long tails, or a flat top with short
ones?".

::: {.callout-note}
#### Definition — kurtosis
**Kurtosis** describes the "tailedness" and peak of a distribution
relative to a normal distribution: **leptokurtic** (heavy tails,
sharp peak), **mesokurtic** (normal-like), **platykurtic** (light
tails, flat peak). In this course, kurtosis is treated
**conceptually only** — names and pictures, no formula, no Excel
function.
:::

## Worked example

Using "The Wandering Fork"'s `daily_revenue_eur` ($n=30$), with
$\bar{x}=628.34$, $Me=643.63$, grouped mode $Mo=666.67$ (Module 4),
$s=137.09$ (Module 6), and $Q_1=506.61$, $Q_3=729.99$,
$IQR=223.39$ (Module 5), all verified in `data-model.md`:

| Statistic | Value | Interpretation |
|---|---:|---|
| Fisher-Pearson sample skewness | +0.034 | near-symmetric, very mild right skew |
| Pearson skewness coefficient | −0.280 | mildly left, per this formula |
| Pearson median form $3(\bar{x}-Me)/s$ | −0.335 | mildly left, per this formula |
| Yule-Kendall skewness coefficient | −0.227 | mildly left, per this formula |

**Step 1 — the headline measure.** The Fisher-Pearson sample
skewness, computed with Excel's `SKEW` on all 30 raw observations, is
$+0.034$. Being so close to zero, this is the course's official
conclusion: "The Wandering Fork"'s daily revenue is **essentially
symmetric**, with only a very slight lean toward high values.

**Step 2 — Pearson asymmetry.** $(\bar{x}-Mo)/s = (628.34-666.67)/137.09
\approx -0.280$: comparing the mean to the *grouped-estimated* mode
instead of using every raw value gives a mildly negative reading. The
median form, $3(628.34-643.63)/137.09 \approx -0.335$, agrees in sign.

**Step 3 — Yule-Kendall.** $(Q_3+Q_1-2Me)/(Q_3-Q_1) =
(729.99+506.61-2\times643.63)/223.39 \approx -0.227$: comparing only
the five-number summary also leans mildly negative.

**Step 4 — reconciling the disagreement.** Steps 2 and 3 lean
slightly negative while Step 1 leans slightly positive. This is not a
contradiction, it is a lesson: the Fisher-Pearson coefficient uses
every one of the 30 raw daily revenues, while the Pearson coefficient
depends on the grouped mode ($Mo=666.67$), itself only an
*estimate* from five class frequencies, and the Yule-Kendall
coefficient uses just four numbers ($Q_1, Me, Q_3$, and the range
between the first two). For a distribution this close to symmetric,
such small formula-specific approximations are enough to flip the
sign — which is itself consistent with the headline conclusion that
the true skew is very small in absolute terms either way. **The
value to report and remember for "The Wandering Fork" is the
Fisher-Pearson $+0.034$.**

### Campus franchise (right-skewed case)

For Campus 120-day revenue: Fisher-Pearson skewness = +1.00, Pearson
median form = +0.63 (Campus revenue has no unique mode, so the median
form is used), Yule-Kendall = +0.15. All three are positive and agree
on **right skew** — the event-driven revenue spikes create a long
upper tail. Yule-Kendall is the weakest because it only looks at the
middle half of the data and ignores the tail beyond $Q_3$. This is
the pattern Module 6's high $CV$ (67.6%) and Module 5's three
outliers were already signaling.

## Proof / derivation

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Derivation — why Excel's `SKEW` includes a bias-correction factor (click to expand)
The conceptually simplest skewness measure is the **third
standardized moment**,
$$
g_1 = \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})^3}
{\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})^2\right)^{3/2}}
= \frac{m_3}{m_2^{3/2}},
$$
the average cubed deviation ($m_3$), rescaled by the standard
deviation cubed (via $m_2^{3/2}$) so the result is unit-free. Cubing
(rather than squaring, as in variance) is what makes this measure
sensitive to *direction*: a value far above the mean and one equally
far below contribute equal-magnitude but opposite-sign terms, so they
do not cancel the way squared deviations would.

However, $g_1$ computed directly from a *sample* is a biased
estimator of the true population skewness — it systematically
under- or overstates it, especially for small $n$. Excel's `SKEW`
applies the standard small-sample correction, replacing $\frac{1}{n}$
with the factor $\frac{n}{(n-1)(n-2)}$ and using the sample standard
deviation $s$ (with its own $n-1$ correction, Module 6) in place of
the population-style $m_2^{1/2}$:
$$
SKEW = \frac{n}{(n-1)(n-2)}\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\frac{x_i-\bar x}{s}\right)^3.
$$
As $n$ grows large, $\frac{n}{(n-1)(n-2)} \to \frac{1}{n}$ and $s \to
m_2^{1/2}$, so $SKEW \to g_1$: the correction matters most for small
samples (like "The Wandering Fork"'s $n=30$) and becomes negligible
for very large ones.
:::

## Visual intuition

On a histogram, skewness is the **direction of the longer tail**: a
right-skewed histogram has its bulk of bars on the left and a thin
tail trailing off to the right (think: most days are ordinary, a few
are exceptionally good); left-skewed is the mirror image. On a
boxplot, skewness shows up as an **off-center median line inside the
box** and **unequal whisker lengths**: if the whisker toward $Q_3$ is
longer than the one toward $Q_1$, that is visual right skew. For "The
Wandering Fork", the near-equal spacing seen in Module 5's boxplot
(median roughly centered between $Q_1=506.61$ and $Q_3=729.99$) is
the visual signature of the near-zero skewness confirmed numerically
here.

The three-truck figure in the hook shows the same readings on
hand-sized data: step 2 shows the mean dragged toward the tail, step 3
shows the far day's cube deciding the sign, and step 4 shows Stadium's
median hugging $Q_1$ while Market's hugs $Q_3$.

## Exercises

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Exercise 1 (by hand) — Reading the sign and magnitude (click for solution)
A distribution has a Fisher-Pearson sample skewness of $-0.85$. What
does the sign and rough magnitude tell you about its shape, and about
the typical ordering of its mean and median?

**Solution.** The negative sign means the distribution is
**left-skewed**: it has a longer or fatter tail toward low values. A
magnitude of $0.85$ (using the common rule of thumb: roughly
$|SKEW|<0.5$ near-symmetric, $0.5$–$1$ moderate skew, $>1$ strong
skew) indicates a **moderate** left skew — noticeable, but not
extreme. In this case, the typical ordering is $\bar{x} < Me < Mo$:
the few low outlying values pull the mean below the median.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Exercise 2 (by hand) — Reconciling mean/median/mode order with the headline skewness (click for solution)
"The Wandering Fork"'s mean (628.34), median (643.63), and grouped
mode (666.67) follow the order $\bar{x} < Me < Mo$, which is the
classic textbook signature of *left* skew — yet the Fisher-Pearson
coefficient reports $+0.034$, a very mild *right* skew. How do you
reconcile this?

**Solution.** The "$\bar{x}<Me<Mo$ implies left skew" rule is only a
rough heuristic, not a guarantee, and it is especially unreliable
here for two reasons: (1) the gaps between the three values are tiny
relative to the spread of the data ($s=137.09$), so their exact order
can flip with negligible changes in the underlying data; and (2) the
mode used is a *grouped estimate* ($Mo=666.67$, from five class
frequencies), not an exact value computed from all 30 raw
observations the way $\bar{x}$, $Me$, and the Fisher-Pearson
coefficient are. The Fisher-Pearson value, using every raw
observation, is the more precise and authoritative measure here, and
at $+0.034$ it confirms the distribution is essentially symmetric —
close enough to zero that a heuristic based on three closely-spaced,
partly-estimated landmarks should not be trusted to override it.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Exercise 3 (by hand) — Yule-Kendall from a five-number summary (click for solution)
A dataset has $Q_1=40$, $Me=50$, $Q_3=55$. Compute the Yule-Kendall
skewness coefficient and interpret its sign.

**Solution.**
$$
YK = \frac{Q_3+Q_1-2Me}{Q_3-Q_1}
= \frac{55+40-2\times50}{55-40}
= \frac{95-100}{15}
= -\frac{5}{15} \approx -0.33.
$$
The negative sign indicates mild **left** skew by this measure: the
median (50) sits closer to $Q_3$ (55) than to $Q_1$ (40), meaning the
lower quarter of the data is more spread out than the upper quarter
— a longer effective "reach" on the low side.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Exercise 4 (by hand) — Formula to words (click for solution)
(a) Read $\dfrac{Q_3+Q_1-2\,Me}{Q_3-Q_1}$ aloud as one sentence.
Which indicator is it?

(b) Read $\dfrac{\bar{x}-Mo}{s}$ aloud, then compute it for a truck
with $\bar{x} = 500$, $Mo = 440$ and $s = 120$. What does the sign
say?

(c) In $\left(\frac{x_i-\bar{x}}{s}\right)^3$, what does dividing by
$s$ do, and what does cubing do?

**Solution.** (a) "Q three plus Q one minus twice the median, divided
by Q three minus Q one" — the Yule-Kendall coefficient $YK$.
(b) "x-bar minus the mode, divided by s" — the Pearson coefficient:
$(500-440)/120 = 60/120 = 0.5$. Positive: the mean is pulled above the
mode, a sign of right skew.
(c) Dividing by $s$ measures the deviation in standard deviations, so
the result has no unit; cubing keeps the sign of the deviation and
makes the far-out values dominate.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Exercise 5 (by hand) — Words to formula (click for solution)
Write in symbols:

(a) "three times the gap between the mean and the median, divided by
the standard deviation";
(b) "the deviation of the $i$-th observation from the mean, measured
in standard deviations, then cubed";
(c) "add up those cubes for all $n$ observations".

**Solution.** (a) $\dfrac{3(\bar{x}-Me)}{s}$ — Pearson's median form.
(b) $\left(\dfrac{x_i-\bar{x}}{s}\right)^3$.
(c) $\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\dfrac{x_i-\bar{x}}{s}\right)^3$ — multiply
it by $\frac{n}{(n-1)(n-2)}$ and you get $SKEW$.
:::

## Common mistakes

::: {.callout-warning}
#### Watch out
- **Reporting "the skewness" without naming the formula.** Always
  specify: Fisher-Pearson (Excel's `SKEW`), Pearson, or Yule-Kendall.
- **Trusting the mean/median/mode ordering heuristic for near-symmetric
  data.** The gaps can be tiny; the Fisher-Pearson coefficient using
  all raw data is the authoritative measure.
- **Using the grouped mode in the Pearson coefficient without stating
  it is an estimate.** The grouped mode is an approximation; the
  Pearson coefficient computed with it inherits that approximation
  error.
- **Confusing kurtosis with skewness.** Skewness = asymmetry
  (lopsided); kurtosis = tailedness/peak (heavy vs light tails).
  This course covers skewness numerically; kurtosis conceptually
  only.
- **Forgetting the small-sample correction in `SKEW`.** Excel's
  `SKEW` includes it automatically; if you implement the formula
  manually, you must include $\frac{n}{(n-1)(n-2)}$.
:::

## Exit check

Five minutes, no calculator needed except for question 4.

1. In one sentence, what does a positive skewness tell you about the
   shape of a distribution?
2. A dataset has mean 42, median 38 and mode 35. Which way is it
   skewed, and on which side is the long tail?
3. Read $SKEW = \frac{n}{(n-1)(n-2)}\sum_{i=1}^{n}
   \left(\frac{x_i-\bar{x}}{s}\right)^3$ aloud as a sentence.
4. Compute the Yule-Kendall coefficient for $Q_1 = 20$, $Me = 24$,
   $Q_3 = 36$.
5. Why are the deviations cubed in the skewness formula instead of
   squared, as in the variance?

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Exit check — answers
1. The distribution has a longer tail toward high values: a few
   unusually high observations pull the mean above the median.
2. Mode < median < mean: right-skewed, with the long tail toward high
   values.
3. "The sum, over all $n$ observations, of each deviation from the
   mean measured in standard deviations and cubed, multiplied by $n$
   over $(n-1)(n-2)$."
4. $YK = (36+20-2\times24)/(36-20) = 8/16 = 0.5$: the median is closer
   to $Q_1$, so mild right skew.
5. A square is always positive, so it cannot tell left from right; a
   cube keeps the sign, so deviations above and below the mean only
   cancel when the distribution is balanced.
:::

## Homework — Excel lab

Reproduce, in Excel, every indicator you computed by hand in class,
with `AVERAGE`, `MEDIAN`, `MODE.SNGL`, `STDEV.S`, `SKEW` and
`QUARTILE.EXC`, then build a complete descriptive-statistics summary
for a quantitative variable, from raw data to shape indicators,
without external guidance.

**Estimated time:** about 50–60 minutes. Any spreadsheet application
works, at home or in a campus computer room.

**Follow-up:** a 10-minute debrief at the start of
[Module 8](module-08.qmd). Bring your Step 0 results and any question
on Homework 1–3.

### Using Excel

The complete list of function names, with their French equivalents, is
on the [Excel functions](excel-functions.qmd) page.

| Concept | Excel function / steps |
|---|---|
| Fisher-Pearson sample skewness | `=SKEW(range)` |
| Pearson skewness coefficient | No direct function — `=(AVERAGE(range)-Mo)/STDEV.S(range)`, with $Mo$ computed manually (Module 4) |
| Yule-Kendall skewness coefficient | No direct function — `=(QUARTILE.EXC(range,3)+QUARTILE.EXC(range,1)-2*MEDIAN(range))/(QUARTILE.EXC(range,3)-QUARTILE.EXC(range,1))` |

For the **full table** (120 days per franchise) use the Excel Table
`tblFork` and add the franchise as one more condition, for example
`=SKEW(FILTER(tblFork[daily_revenue_eur], tblFork[franchise]="Campus"))`.

### Step 0 — check your class results

1. Type Station's six values (510, 570, 600, 600, 630, 690) in
   `A2:A7`, Stadium's five (550, 550, 580, 630, 690) in `B2:B6` and
   Market's five (510, 570, 620, 650, 650) in `C2:C6`.
2. Below each column, compute `=AVERAGE(A2:A7)`, `=MEDIAN(A2:A7)`,
   `=MODE.SNGL(A2:A7)`, `=STDEV.S(A2:A7)`, `=SKEW(A2:A7)`,
   `=QUARTILE.EXC(A2:A7,1)` and `=QUARTILE.EXC(A2:A7,3)`. Repeat for
   columns B and C (rows 2 to 6).
3. From those cells, compute the Pearson coefficient
   (mean − mode) / s, the median form 3 × (mean − median) / s and the
   Yule-Kendall coefficient with the formulas of the table above.
4. Compare every result with your hand-computed tables.

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Step 0 — expected results
| Indicator | Station | Stadium | Market |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `AVERAGE` | 600 | 600 | 600 |
| `MEDIAN` | 600 | 580 | 620 |
| `MODE.SNGL` | 600 | 550 | 650 |
| `STDEV.S` | 60 | 60 | 60 |
| `SKEW` | 0 | 0.96 | −0.96 |
| `QUARTILE.EXC(…,1)` | 555 | 550 | 540 |
| `QUARTILE.EXC(…,3)` | 645 | 660 | 650 |
| Pearson $(\bar{x}-Mo)/s$ | 0 | 0.83 | −0.83 |
| Pearson median form | 0 | 1.00 | −1.00 |
| Yule-Kendall | 0 | 0.45 | −0.45 |

Station's `SKEW` may show a tiny number such as `1E-16` instead of 0:
that is rounding noise in the computer, not real skew.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Homework 1 (Excel) — Skewness for Campus revenue (click for solution)
In `wandering-fork.xlsx`, filter `franchise` to "Campus" and compute
`=SKEW` for `daily_revenue_eur` (120 days). Also compute the Pearson
(median form, since there is no unique mode) and Yule-Kendall
coefficients. Do all three agree on the direction?

**How to.** Wrap the range in
`FILTER(tblFork[daily_revenue_eur], tblFork[franchise]="Campus")`
inside `SKEW`, `AVERAGE`, `MEDIAN`, `STDEV.S` and `QUARTILE.EXC`, then
type the two coefficient formulas of the Using Excel table.

**Solution.** Campus 120-day: `SKEW` = 1.00, Pearson median form =
$3(455.03-390.39)/307.43 \approx 0.63$, Yule-Kendall =
$(598.60+236.07-2\times390.39)/362.54 \approx 0.15$. All three are
**positive**, confirming right skew — consistent with the
event-driven revenue spikes and the three outliers found in Module 5.
Yule-Kendall is much smaller because the long tail lies beyond $Q_3$,
where it cannot see.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Homework 2 (Excel) — Payroll skew: skewness (click for solution)
Open `payroll-skew.csv`. Compute the Fisher-Pearson skewness for the
11 salaries. What does the value tell you?

**How to.** Open the CSV, select the 11 salaries and type
`=SKEW(range)`; add `=AVERAGE(range)` and `=MEDIAN(range)` to compare.

**Solution.** `SKEW` = 3.12. This is **strong right skew** — the
CEO's €180,000 salary creates an extremely long upper tail. The mean
(€47,231) is far above the median (€38,050), and the mode (no unique
mode) would be even lower. This is the most skewed dataset in the
course.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Homework 3 (Excel) — Full univariate workflow for Campus revenue (click for solution)
Using `wandering-fork.xlsx` filtered to "Campus" (120 days), build a
complete descriptive summary for `daily_revenue_eur` in one
continuous Excel workflow: class table (Module 3), quartiles and
boxplot (Module 5), mean/median/mode (Module 4), variance/std/CV
(Module 6), skewness (this module). Verify internal consistency
(e.g., $Q_1 \le Me \le Q_3$, mean ≈ median for symmetric data).

**How to.** Work on one sheet, one block per module, reusing the
functions of each module's Using Excel table, and finish with the
consistency checks.

**Solution.** Campus 120-day summary:
- Class table: 8 classes of width 200 (Module 3, Exercise 4), modal
  class [200,400[ (37 days), long tail up to [1400,1600[
- Quartiles: Q1=236.07, Me=390.39, Q3=598.60, IQR=362.54, fences
  -307.74 / 1142.40, three high outliers (1335.48, 1362.93, 1407.59)
- Mean=455.03, median=390.39, no unique mode
- Variance=94,511.80, std=307.43, CV=67.56%
- Skewness=1.00 (right-skewed)
